content: 68W, commonly referred to as 68 Whiskey using the phonetic alphabet, is the Military Occupational Specialty (MOS) designation for healthcare specialists in the United States Army, also known as combat medics. The primary responsibility of a 68W is to provide medical care to injured soldiers. These medics are integral to the operational effectiveness of the Army, as every squad is required to have a combat medic present during hazardous missions. They are involved in all stages of medical care in combat zones, starting from the point of injury, continuing through evacuation to medical facilities, and extending to treatment within those facilities. 68W personnel are highly trained to perform medical duties in challenging and dangerous environments. They work under the supervision of Army Physician Assistants (PAs) or doctors, performing a wide range of tasks. These include administering immunizations, collecting fluid samples, obtaining vital signs, gathering initial patient information, treating trauma, assisting in surgeries, and suturing wounds. In the absence of other medical professionals, they are trained to provide Basic Life Support (BLS) and maintain patient stability. In clinical settings, 68Ws can serve as senior enlisted personnel, such as Platoon Sergeants in medical platoons, or as leaders in clinics. They are also responsible for conducting training and counseling sessions for soldiers, ensuring readiness for patient care and self-improvement. The MOS is continually evolving to enhance the capabilities of healthcare specialists. The civilian equivalent of a 68W is an Emergency Medical Technician-Basic (EMT-B). With additional training, such as courses through Mountain State University, they may earn an Associate's Degree in medical assisting. Some universities also offer technical degrees in Emergency Medical Sciences, allowing 68Ws to further their medical careers. Many 68Ws pursue advanced roles such as Physician Assistants, Nurse Practitioners, Registered Nurses, Doctors, or Healthcare Administrators through continued education and training. The rank structure for 68Ws includes: 68W10: Entry-level combat medic 68W20: Sergeant (E-5) 68W30: Staff Sergeant (E-6) 68W40: Sergeant First Class (E-7) 68W50: Master Sergeant/First Sergeant (E-8) or Sergeant Major (E-9) Skill identifiers for 68Ws include: F6: Army Flight Medic M6: Licensed Practical Nurse P6: Orthopedics Specialist Y8: Immunization-Allergy Specialist N3: Occupational Therapy Assistant N9: Physical Therapy Technician Y2: Identifier for those who have not completed upgrade training W1: Special Operations Combat Medic (SOCM) P3: Optometry Specialist Y6: Cardiovascular Specialist Historically, the MOS was known as 91W, with earlier designations of 91B (91 Bravo) and 91A (91 Alpha). The transition to 68W began on October 1, 2001, and was completed by September 30, 2007. During this period, medics were required to complete EMT-B certification, which had not been mandatory before. Failure to meet these standards led to some medics being reclassified into other MOSs. Training for 68Ws occurs after basic training at Fort Sam Houston, where they undergo Advanced Individual Training (AIT) for 16 to 68 weeks, depending on their skill identifier. This training includes a variety of medical tasks essential for their military careers. To maintain their MOS, 68Ws must obtain and renew EMT and CPR certifications, which require ongoing training throughout their careers. They may also attend advanced courses tailored to their unit's functional role, such as advanced trauma treatments or medication administration. Combat medics attached to field hospital units often perform duties typically assigned to Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) due to the limited availability of M6 personnel. Some medics pursue advanced certifications like EMT-Intermediate or EMT-Paramedic, or attend the Army's Interservice Physician Assistant Program (IPAP) to become PAs. Others may choose to specialize further, such as becoming Special Forces Medical Sergeants (18D) or Special Operations Combat Medics (SOCM), who are among the most independent-duty enlisted medical personnel in the Army. SOCM-qualified 68Ws serve in elite units such as the 75th Ranger Regiment, 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment (SOAR), and Civil Affairs Battalions. They operate under specific protocols with a limited scope of practice, often in the absence of medical officers. Their training includes advanced medical and military courses to enhance interoperability with other special operations soldiers. Responsibilities of 68Ws include: Providing cover fire to incapacitate enemies Accompanying patrols to deliver immediate medical care in combat Stabilizing and triaging casualties Planning and conducting medical evacuations and en route life support Implementing preventive medicine and field sanitation Delivering clinical medicine and supportive care during delayed transport Training unit personnel in Combat Lifesaver (CLS) programs Combat Lifesaver training equips non-medical soldiers with emergency medical skills to provide point-of-wounding care and act as a bridge between self-aid or buddy aid and the combat medic. These skills are designed for use in combat conditions but can also be applied in non-combat scenarios. The doctrine aims to increase survivability in situations where a combat medic may not be immediately available.
